newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China policy shift means more crude imports.
newsitem.headline: China policy shift means more crude imports.

text.p: Coastal Chinese refineries, squeezed by higher domestic prices and a policy shift directing more oil to inland refineries, will increase crude imports this year, refinery officials said on Thursday.
These refineries could add at least one million tonnes to China's annual crude imports in 1997, estimated by state media in January at 34 million tonnes, they said.
The media estimate indicated a rise of more than 50 percent from 22.62 million tonnes in 1996, although analysts said they did not expect imports to rise so sharply.
"The state policy is to narrow the gap between international and domestic prices and allow inland refineries to get more supplies," an official of state refiner Sinopec said from Beijing.
"We have to comply with international standards. We can't always offer subsidies to domestic companies," said another Sinopec official.

In December, the China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) raised the price it sells crude to Sinopec by 86.8 yuan (US$10.4) per tonne to around 1,085 yuan per tonne as part of its drive to end perferential prices.
The state-subsidised price was around 300 yuan per tonne in the early 1980s, Chinese company sources said.
Sinopec is China's biggest refiner, accounting for more than 80 percent of the country's total refining capacity of 4.3 million barrels per day (bpd).
However, bringing an end to preferrential prices is expected to force refineries to import more crude themselves as the prices become less attractive, Chinese company sources said.

Sinopec supplied 4.5 million tonnes of crude at around 1,000 yuan per tonne to Shanghai Petrochemical Company (SPC) in 1996 and the amount will be cut by one million tonnes, or 22 percent, in 1997, a SPC official said from Shanghai.
"In the past we didn't have to import any crude. We relied solely on Sinopec. But this year we have to start importing crude ourselves," the official said.
The preferrential price, now 10-20 percent lower than market prices, is expected to go up by about 100 yuan per tonne in 1997, the official said.
"The price has been going up year by year and it definitely will continue rising and incease our crude purchase cost," the official said.
Zhenhai Refining and Chemical Co based in coastal Zhejiang province, with more than 20 percent of its crude supplied by Sinopec, is ready to raise crude imports.
"We have been informed (of the supply cut) and we are ready to import more crude ourselves," said an official at the Zhenhai refinery, which needs seven million tonnes annually.
Zhenhai's import increase would depend on Sinopec's supply cut and could differ from season to season, the official said.

"Sinopec aims to make coastal refineries import more crude themselves because of geographical convenience and provide more crude to inland refineries," said an official at China's state importer China National Chemicals Import and Export Co (Sinochem) in Singapore.

"One million tonnes (from SPC) is not a big amount for imports, but the likely result is those companies may be forced to raise product prices after self-imports increase their cost," the official said.
(US$1 = 8.3 yuan)
-- Singapore newsroom (65-8703571)
